catalog_quote: Assignment of stress in Punjabi is entirely predictable, yet it patterns differently in disyllabic and trisyllabic words. [p. 84] ... Punjabi exhibits a three-way distinction in syllable weight with monomoraic light syllables, bimoraic heavy syllables, and trimoraic superheavy syllables. [p. 84] ... In Punjabi, secondary stress is not found and main stress is not contrastive. ... Stress is also not affected by morphology. ... stress in Punjabi is distributed solely according to a pattern based on the weight of the syllables contained within a word. [p. 85] ... An exhaustive list of stress patterns for disyllabic words is shown in (4) and for trisyllabic words in (5). new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (12 pp., text layer; also rendered pp. 85-86 as images because the text layer drops the acute accents). Each quoted fragment is present at the stated locator: p. 84 sec. 0 'Assignment of stress in Punjabi is entirely predictable, yet it patterns differently in disyllabic and trisyllabic words.' (verbatim); p. 85 'In Punjabi, secondary stress is not found and main stress is not contrastive.' and 'stress in Punjabi is distributed solely according to a pattern based on the weight of the syllables contained within a word.' (verbatim); p. 85 'An exhaustive list of stress patterns for disyllabic words is shown in (4) and for trisyllabic words in (5)'; exx. (4)-(5) on pp. 85-86 show exactly…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, non-contrastive single word stress with a three-way weight scale (L = CV, H = CVV/CVC, S = CVVC/CVCC). Disyllables: a superheavy syllable takes stress (the first if both are S; final stress only when the final is S and the initial is not); otherwise stress is initial (ĹH, H́H). Trisyllables: a final superheavy is skipped; stress the penult if it is heavy or superheavy (HH́H, LH́H, LŚH, HŚH), otherwise the antepenult (ĹLH, H́LH, H́HS, ĹHS). Analysed as moraic trochees built right-to-left with the leftmost foot stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly none: 'secondary stress is not found' (p. 85).
new_statements.exceptions: Dhillon: morphology (verb suffixes, plural) does not shift stress; rejects Arun 1961/Bhatia 1993 minimal pairs (galaa 'throat' vs galáa 'melt') as geminate-medial vs vowel-deleted monosyllables; notes Vijayakrishnan 2003 lists an HLŚ pattern unattested in his dialect. Other sources differ in detail: Bajaj 2019 (Malwai, p. 62) states penult default, ultima only if extra-heavy and penult not, antepenult if penult light (or all three heavy), reapplying after affixation; Tolstaya 1981/Kalra 1982/Bhatia 1993 (per Bajaj) report final stress on imperatives/causatives and on suffixes -vālā, -hār, -dār, -kār; Gill & Gleason 1962 describe the same facts as tone-onset placement on 1st vs 2nd syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level main stress in citation forms (di- and trisyllables; polysyllables not treated by Dhillon). Tone docks on the stressed syllable (Bailey 1914, Arun 1961, Bajaj 2019). Dialect: Majhi of villages near Amritsar, India.
new_statements.identity_note: Dhillon 2007 describes the Majhi dialect spoken in villages near Amritsar, India (the prestige basis of standard Eastern Panjabi, panj1256). Bajaj 2019 describes spoken Malwai (Malwa region, Indian Punjab), also under panj1256. Gill & Gleason 1962 and Arun 1961 describe literary/standard Indian Panjabi; Jain 1934 describes Ludhiani (Malwai/Powadhi border). Bashir & Conners 2019 (list of works to obtain) describe Lahore Panjabi, which is linguistically Majhi but is filed by ISO under Western Panjabi [pnb]; Hussain et al. 2020 describe Lyallpuri (Faisalabad, Pakistan).

In Punjabi, secondary stress is not found and main stress is not contrastive. ... stress in Punjabi is distributed solely according to a pattern based on the weight of the syllables contained within a word. [p.85] ... An exhaustive list of stress patterns for disyllabic words ... (4) ĹH pɛ́.laa 'before/earlier', H́H kə́n.daa 'thorn', ŚH, ŚS, LŚ, HŚ ... (5) ĹLH, H́LH, H́HS, ĹHS, HH́H, LH́H, LŚH, HŚH [pp.85-86] ... Punjabi has a preference for stressing superheavy syllables, tends to avoid assigning stress to final positions [p.92]
sources.note: Stress entirely predictable, not contrastive, no secondary stress, morphology irrelevant; three-way weight (L/H/S); exhaustive patterns: disyllables ĹH, H́H, ŚH, ŚS, LŚ, HŚ; trisyllables ĹLH, H́LH, H́HS, ĹHS, HH́H, LH́H, LŚH, HŚH; preference for superheavies, avoid final stress; moraic trochees R-to-L, leftmost foot stressed (pp. 84-92). Argues Arun 1961/Bhatia 1993 'contrastive stress' pairs are mis-analysed.

sources.citation: Bajaj, Mansi. 2019. Different Aspects of Punjabi Phonology. PhD thesis, University of Delhi (Shodhganga hdl 10603/432643). [Malwai]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ch. 4 reviews Kalra 1982 (rightmost non-final heavy, else leftmost), Malik 1995, Bahri 2011, Gargesh 1999, Singh 2004, Bhatia 1993; own acoustic study (duration, f0, amplitude; accented syllable = L*, lower f0, longer). Rules p. 62: monosyllables accented; disyllables penult unless ultima extra-heavy and penult not; trisyllables+ penult unless penult light and antepenult not, or all three heavy -> antepenult; reapplies after resyllabification.

sources.citation: Joshi, Shiv Sharma. 1978. The phonology of the verbal phrase in Punjabi (Doabi). PhD thesis, University of London (SOAS).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Firthian prosodic study of verb words; stress marked and tied to tone exponency; notes causative stems have stress 'ultimate in disyllabic stems and penultimate in trisyllabic words' (e.g. [lebá] vs [lebána]); no general word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Gill, Harjeet Singh & Henry A. Gleason Jr. 1962. A Reference Grammar of Panjabi. Hartford Studies in Linguistics 3. Hartford Seminary Foundation (ERIC ED013359).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No 'stress' category; prominence handled as tone: every word has exactly one tone onset, on the 1st or 2nd syllable; 2nd-syllable onset when syll 1 has a centralized vowel, syll 2 a peripheral vowel and the intervening C is single (or /r ṛ n ɳ/), and in some tatsamas; otherwise initial (sec. 3.4 Tone Placement, pp. 48-50). Functionally a weight-conditioned accent-placement statement.

sources.citation: Arun, Vidya Bhaskar. 1961. A Comparative Phonology of Hindi and Panjabi. Ludhiana: Panjabi Sahitya Akademi.

sources.note: §59 (p. 36): 'Although stress is not a prominent feature of Panjabi, it is, however, sometimes phonemic' with pairs gala 'throat' / galá 'melt!' etc; §60: tone always falls on the stressed syllable; in trisyllabics the second syllable 'is invariably stressed'. No general placement algorithm.

sources.citation: Jain, Banarsi Das. 1934. A Phonology of Panjabi as spoken about Ludhiana and a Ludhiani Phonetic Reader. Lahore: University of the Panjab.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Phonetic Reader §§83-84 (p. 166): Ludhiani has a 'pseudo-stress' (length+pitch, not force), illustrated by pairs 'tʌṛka vs taṛ'ka:, 'rala vs ra'la: etc; no placement rule. Historical part §182 (p. 94): accent shifted to the initial syllable except where a non-final syllable has a long vowel, then on the last such; §191: recent loans/tatsamas show penultimate accent.
